Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)  -- The Taliban in Afghanistan have momentum that makes any effort to negotiate with them difficult, the U.S. defense secretary said. Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday. He's visiting Afghanistan on Wednesday. Secretary Robert Gates spoke to CNN's Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before leaving for Afghanistan, where he is visiting troops and bases Wednesday. "The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point," Gates said in the interview. "They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult." As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and Afghanistan government are attempting to reach out to elements of the Taliban who are engaged in the battle for financial gain, rather than ideological gain. "There are really two groups we're talking about -- the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed. The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we'll probably have to wait awhile before there's an opportunity there." On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson interviewed a spokesman for the Taliban, Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban will only negotiate with the Afghanistan government when the United States leaves the country. "Our conditions are clear, we want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country," Mujahid told CNN. Gates said the stance was not surprising. "Well I don't know what else he'd say. He's leading the opposition, he's leading this insurgency. He's not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say 'We're ready to negotiate, we're about done here,' " Gates said. The United States is adding 21,000 troops to the Afghanistan battlefield. The majority will be moving to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border. The Taliban have had mostly free rein in that area with few U.S. or coalition forces to confront them until now. Gates admitted moving the battle to the south will mean there is "a tough fight ahead." "I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we're clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched," he said. "And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties." In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has seen the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that the increased fighting in southern Afghanistan will only push the Taliban back to the Pakistani side. "Well I think it's just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy," Gates said. Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperation efforts between the two countries to deal with the problem, and by Pakistan's recent confrontation with the Taliban in Bunir province, near the capital of Islamabad. "The signs right now are pretty positive," he told CNN.

outputs.L1:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN) — The Taliban in Afghanistan possess a momentum that renders any effort to negotiate with them exceedingly difficult, the U.S. defense secretary said. Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and is scheduled to visit Afghanistan on Wednesday.

Secretary Gates spoke with CNN's Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview on Tuesday evening, prior to his departure for Afghanistan, where he will visit troops and military bases on Wednesday.

"The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to contemplate reconciliation or any form of accommodation at this point," Gates said in the interview. "They likely believe that the momentum is on their side. And until that momentum shifts, it will remain difficult."

As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and the Afghan government are seeking to engage elements of the Taliban who participate in the conflict for financial rather than ideological reasons.

"There are really two groups we're addressing—the younger, or less committed, who do this primarily to earn a living and provide for their families, and those who are more ideologically driven. The latter will prove far more challenging to reach, and we will likely have to wait some time before an opportunity presents itself."

On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson interviewed Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who stated that the Taliban would negotiate with the Afghan government only after the United States withdrew from the country.

"Our conditions are clear: we are willing to negotiate, provided they [the U.S.] do not interfere in our affairs; and secondly, they [the U.S.] must leave the country," Mujahid told CNN.

Gates said this position came as no surprise. "Well, I don't know what else he would say. He's leading the opposition; he's leading this insurgency. He's hardly going to lay down his arms and declare, 'We're ready to negotiate, we're just about finished here,'" Gates remarked.

The United States is deploying an additional 21,000 troops to the Afghan battlefield. The majority will move south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border—a region where the Taliban have operated with near-impunity, facing few U.S. or coalition forces until now.

Gates acknowledged that shifting the battle southward would entail "a tough fight ahead."

"I think I have been quite clear on this. As we move into areas of the south that have not yet seen any Afghan or coalition forces, we will clearly be entering regions where the Taliban are deeply entrenched," he said. "And, regrettably, I anticipate that with the rising level of our activity and operations, casualties will probably be higher."

In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has witnessed the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have voiced concern to the United States that the intensified fighting in southern Afghanistan will merely drive the Taliban back onto the Pakistani side.

"Well, I think it's simply the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So, like it or not, the two nations share a common enemy," Gates said.

Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperative efforts between the two countries to address the problem, as well as by Pakistan's recent confrontation with the Taliban in Buner province, near the capital of Islamabad.

"The signs at present are quite positive," he told CNN.

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)** -- According to the U.S. defense secretary, the Taliban in Afghanistan currently hold a level of momentum that complicates any attempts at negotiation.

Robert Gates, who touched down in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and planned to travel to Afghanistan on Wednesday, sat down with CNN's Chris Lawrence for an exclusive conversation on Tuesday evening. This interview took place just before his departure to Afghanistan, where he intended to meet with troops and inspect military bases on Wednesday.

"At this stage, the Taliban's political leadership is likely unwilling to consider reconciliation or compromise of any sort," Gates remarked during the discussion. "They probably believe that momentum is on their side. That will remain a challenge until such momentum shifts."

A component of American strategy involves both the military and the Afghan government attempting to connect with Taliban members who fight for money rather than out of ideological conviction.

"We're essentially dealing with two distinct groups—those who are younger or less devoted and participate primarily to make a living and feed their families, and those driven more strongly by ideology. Reaching the second group will prove far harder, and we may need to be patient before any chance emerges there," Gates explained.

On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson spoke with Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who stated that the Taliban would agree to talks with the Afghan government only after American forces departed the country. "Our terms are straightforward: we're willing to negotiate provided they [the U.S.] stay out of our matters; and secondly, they [the U.S.] must exit the country," Mujahid said to CNN.

Gates found the position unremarkable. "Honestly, what else would you expect him to say? He heads the opposition and directs this insurgency. He's hardly going to give up and announce, 'We're prepared to negotiate, we're basically finished here,'" Gates observed.

The U.S. is deploying an additional 21,000 troops to the Afghan conflict. Most of these forces will head south to face the Taliban along the porous frontier with Pakistan—an area where the Taliban have operated with little resistance, encountering few U.S. or coalition troops until this point.

Gates acknowledged that shifting the conflict southward would result in "a tough fight ahead."

"I believe I've been quite direct about this. As we advance into southern regions that haven't yet encountered Afghan or coalition forces, we'll obviously be entering territory where the Taliban are deeply established," he said. "And, regrettably, as our operations and activity intensify, I anticipate the casualty numbers will likely climb."

Over the past several weeks, the Pakistani government has watched the Taliban seize control on its portion of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Behind closed doors, Pakistani officials have voiced worries to the U.S. that intensified combat in southern Afghanistan would simply drive the Taliban back across into Pakistan.

"I think it's simply the truth that extremists exist on both sides of that border. They pose a danger to both the elected Afghan government and the elected Pakistani government. So whether they welcome it or not, the two share a common adversary," Gates said.

Gates noted that he takes encouragement from recent collaborative efforts between the two nations aimed at addressing the issue, as well as Pakistan's recent clash with the Taliban in Bunir province, located close to the capital, Islamabad.

"At the moment, the indications are fairly positive," he told CNN.

# U.S. Strategy on Taliban Negotiations Faces Challenges

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates acknowledged that the Taliban's current battlefield momentum has made the prospect of negotiations particularly difficult. According to Gates, insurgents are unlikely to seriously consider reconciliation efforts while they perceive themselves to be holding the upper hand in the conflict.

Despite these challenges, the United States and the Afghan government have developed a strategy aimed at weakening the insurgency from within. Central to this approach is an effort to reach out to less committed Taliban fighters—those who have joined the movement for financial reasons rather than out of ideological conviction. By offering these individuals alternatives, officials hope to reduce the Taliban's overall fighting strength.

Gates drew a clear distinction between two groups within the Taliban ranks. The first consists of younger fighters who have taken up arms primarily as a means of earning a living. The second group is made up of those who are far more ideologically committed to the Taliban's cause and, consequently, much harder to win over through reconciliation efforts. The U.S. strategy focuses on the former group, viewing them as more likely to abandon the insurgency under the right circumstances.

The Taliban, however, has signaled resistance to negotiations under current conditions. A Taliban spokesman, Zabiullah Mujahid, stated that the group will only enter into talks with the Afghan government after the United States has withdrawn its forces from the country. This position underscores the significant gap between the two sides and highlights the obstacles facing any near-term reconciliation.

Meanwhile, the United States is intensifying its military commitment in Afghanistan. As part of its ongoing effort, the U.S. is deploying an additional 21,000 troops to the battlefield, reflecting a determination to shift the momentum of the conflict even as diplomatic pathways remain uncertain.

# The Challenges of Negotiating with the Taliban

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently addressed the complex and often frustrating challenges surrounding the prospect of negotiating with the Taliban in Afghanistan. In his remarks, Gates outlined the nuanced strategy American forces have adopted in approaching the possibility of reconciliation, emphasizing that not all members of the insurgency should be viewed through the same lens.

Central to this strategy is the distinction the United States draws between different types of fighters within the Taliban's ranks. Gates explained that a significant portion of those taking up arms against coalition and Afghan government forces are motivated primarily by financial considerations rather than deep ideological conviction. These fighters, often driven by economic desperation and the need to provide for their families, represent individuals who could potentially be reconciled and reintegrated into Afghan society through the right incentives and opportunities. In contrast, Gates acknowledged that there exists a harder core of Taliban members whose commitment stems from genuine ideological zeal. This group, bound by religious and political conviction, would prove far more difficult to sway or bring to the negotiating table.

Despite outlining this framework for potential reconciliation, Gates offered a candid and sobering assessment of the current situation. He acknowledged that the Taliban's present momentum on the battlefield makes meaningful political reconciliation unlikely at this stage. As long as the insurgents believe they hold the upper hand militarily, they have little incentive to pursue a negotiated settlement or make the compromises that reconciliation would require. From a position of perceived strength, the Taliban sees no pressing reason to abandon armed struggle in favor of political dialogue.

This stalemate was further underscored by the response of a Taliban spokesman, who dismissed the notion of imminent negotiations. The spokesman insisted that the United States must first withdraw its forces from Afghanistan before any talks could even begin. This precondition highlights the fundamental gulf separating the two sides and reinforces Gates's assessment that the conditions for genuine reconciliation have not yet materialized. With each side maintaining incompatible demands, the path toward a political resolution remains obstructed, leaving the conflict to continue playing out on the battlefield for the foreseeable future.

# Riyadh: The Heart of Saudi Arabia

Riyadh stands as the vibrant capital and largest city of Saudi Arabia, serving as the nation's political, economic, and administrative center. Located in the heart of the Arabian Peninsula, this dynamic metropolis has transformed from a modest desert settlement into one of the most influential cities in the Middle East.

## A City of Rapid Growth

Over the past few decades, Riyadh has experienced remarkable development. With a population exceeding seven million people, it has become a bustling urban landscape where traditional Arabian heritage meets cutting-edge modernity. Towering skyscrapers, including the iconic Kingdom Centre and Al Faisaliah Tower, dominate the skyline, symbolizing the city's economic ambitions.

## Economic Powerhouse

As the financial hub of Saudi Arabia, Riyadh plays a crucial role in the country's economy. The city hosts numerous multinational corporations, banks, and government institutions. Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 initiative has further accelerated Riyadh's growth, aiming to diversify the economy beyond oil dependency and establish the city as a global business destination.

## Cultural Heritage

Despite its modern advancements, Riyadh remains deeply connected to its roots. Historical sites such as Diriyah, the original home of the Saudi royal family, and Masmak Fortress offer glimpses into the region's rich past. The National Museum showcases the cultural and historical significance of Saudi Arabia, attracting visitors from around the world.

## A Vision for the Future

Riyadh continues to evolve as Saudi Arabia pursues ambitious modernization goals. From entertainment developments to infrastructure projects like the Riyadh Metro, the city is positioning itself as a leading global capital. As Saudi Arabia opens its doors to international tourism and investment, Riyadh stands at the forefront of this exciting transformation, embodying the nation's aspirations for a prosperous and diversified future.

# Gates: Taliban Momentum Must Be Reversed Before Meaningful Talks

**KABUL, Afghanistan** — Defense Secretary Robert Gates said during a visit to Afghanistan that the Taliban's battlefield momentum must be blunted before any productive reconciliation talks can take place, underscoring the challenges facing U.S. and coalition forces as they seek a political resolution to the long-running conflict.

Speaking to reporters during his trip, Gates acknowledged that while reconciliation with elements of the Taliban remains a possible path toward ending the war, insurgent leaders are unlikely to negotiate seriously while they believe they hold the upper hand.

"The Taliban have to feel themselves under military pressure, and begin to believe that they can't win before they're willing to have a serious conversation," Gates said, reflecting the administration's view that diplomacy and military operations must work in tandem.

## Battlefield Gains

Gates pointed to recent operations in southern Afghanistan, particularly in the Taliban strongholds of Helmand and Kandahar provinces, as evidence that coalition and Afghan forces have begun to reverse insurgent gains. The troop surge ordered by President Obama placed additional forces in these contested regions.

Still, the defense secretary cautioned against overconfidence, noting that gains remain fragile and could be reversed without sustained pressure. He emphasized that the coming months would be critical in determining whether the security improvements could hold.

## The Difficulty of Negotiations

Gates was candid about the obstacles to any negotiated settlement. Distinguishing between rank-and-file fighters who might be persuaded to lay down their arms and hardened senior leadership, he suggested that reconciliation efforts would be complex and uneven.

Any political settlement, Gates reiterated, would need to meet certain conditions: the Taliban must renounce violence, break ties with al Qaeda, and accept the Afghan constitution.

## Looking Ahead

The defense secretary's comments came amid ongoing discussions about the pace of the U.S. drawdown and the transition of security responsibilities to Afghan forces. Gates expressed cautious optimism that progress on the ground could eventually create conditions for a political process, while stressing that the path forward would require continued patience and commitment.

His visit reflected the delicate balance the administration sought to strike between military operations and the pursuit of a long-term political solution to the conflict.

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a realistic news report covering an exclusive interview with U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates about the U.S. troop surge in southern Afghanistan and prospects for Taliban reconciliation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Gates: Afghanistan Surge Aims to Reverse Taliban Momentum, Open Door to Reconciliation

**KABUL** — U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the influx of American troops into southern Afghanistan is designed to break the Taliban's momentum and create conditions that could eventually draw lower-level insurgents away from the fight, in an exclusive interview during his visit to the region.

Speaking aboard his military aircraft and later at a forward operating base in Helmand Province, Gates struck a tone of cautious optimism, emphasizing that battlefield gains must precede any meaningful political settlement.

"The purpose of the surge is straightforward," Gates said. "We need to reverse the Taliban's momentum in their heartland — Helmand and Kandahar — and give the Afghan government and its security forces the breathing room to establish credible governance. Military pressure and reconciliation are not contradictory. One enables the other."

## Reversing the Tide in the South

The additional forces, part of the broader troop buildup ordered by the White House, have concentrated in the Taliban strongholds of southern Afghanistan, where coalition and Afghan units have pushed into districts long contested by insurgents.

Gates acknowledged the campaign would be difficult and that casualties were likely to rise in the near term as forces moved into areas the Taliban had controlled for years.

"I won't sugarcoat it. This is going to be hard, and it's going to be bloody at times," he said. "But we are seeing the beginnings of a shift. The question is whether we can hold and build on what we clear — that's where the Afghan government has to step up."

He praised the performance of U.S. Marines and NATO partners in the region but stressed that the ultimate measure of success would be the ability of Afghan forces to hold territory independently.

## Distinguishing Reconciliation from Reintegration

On the politically sensitive question of dealing with the Taliban, Gates drew a careful distinction between high-level "reconciliation" with senior insurgent leaders and the "reintegration" of rank-and-file fighters.

"There are a lot of people who are fighting for reasons that have nothing to do with ideology," Gates said. "They fight because they're paid, because they're intimidated, or because they have local grievances. Those men can be brought back into society if the security situation improves and there are viable alternatives."

He was more reserved on the prospect of negotiating with the Taliban's senior leadership, saying any such talks would have to be led by the Afghan government and would depend on insurgents meeting basic conditions.

"Reconciliation at the top level is ultimately an Afghan process, not an American one," Gates said. "But our position is clear: anyone who wants to be part of a political solution has to renounce violence, break with al-Qaeda, and accept the Afghan constitution. Short of that, there's not much to talk about."

## Pressure First, Then Politics

Gates repeatedly returned to the theme that a position of strength was a prerequisite for any political outcome, warning against the assumption that insurgents would negotiate seriously while they believed they were winning.

"History shows that insurgencies don't come to the table when they think they're on the ascent," he said. "You reconcile from strength, not weakness. That's precisely why the military effort matters so much right now."

Asked about timelines, Gates cautioned against expecting rapid results, noting that the effects of the troop increase would take months to become clear and that governance improvements would take longer still.

## Concerns Over Governance and Corruption

Pressed on persistent concerns about corruption and weak governance within the Afghan administration, Gates conceded that these remained among the most serious obstacles to lasting success.

"Military operations can only buy time and space," he said. "If that space isn't filled by honest, functioning government that delivers for ordinary Afghans, then we're just mowing the grass. The Afghan leadership understands this is their responsibility, and we will keep pressing them on it."

## Looking Ahead

As his visit concluded, Gates expressed confidence in the overall strategy while acknowledging the American public's growing impatience with a war stretching into its second decade.

"I'm realistic about the challenges, and I'm realistic about the patience of the American people," he said. "But I believe we now have the right strategy and the right resources. What we need is the resolve to see it through — and the wisdom to know that the end of this war will look more like a political settlement than a battlefield victory."

*This report is a fictional composition created for illustrative purposes and does not represent an actual interview or verbatim statements.*

# Gates: Reconciliation With Some Taliban Possible as U.S. Boosts Afghan Force

**Defense Secretary outlines strategy amid troop surge, border security concerns**

WASHINGTON — Defense Secretary Robert Gates suggested that reconciliation with elements of the Taliban could eventually become part of a broader political solution in Afghanistan, even as the United States moves forward with a significant increase in troop levels to combat a resurgent insurgency.

Speaking to reporters, Gates drew a distinction between hardcore Taliban fighters and those who might be persuaded to lay down their arms and reintegrate into Afghan society. The comments reflect a nuanced approach that mirrors reconciliation efforts credited with helping reduce violence in Iraq.

## A Political Component to the Fight

"There has to be ultimately, and I'll underscore ultimately, reconciliation as part of a political outcome to this," Gates said, emphasizing that any such process would be led by the Afghan government rather than dictated by Washington.

Gates acknowledged that the situation remains complex, drawing careful lines between those who could potentially be brought into the political fold and irreconcilable extremists committed to violence. The approach recognizes that not all who fight under the Taliban banner share the same ideological commitment, with some driven by economic desperation, tribal loyalties, or coercion.

The Defense Secretary's remarks came at a time when the Obama administration was reviewing its overall strategy for the region, seeking to balance military pressure with political and diplomatic tools.

## 21,000 Additional Troops

Central to the military component of the strategy is the deployment of approximately 21,000 additional American troops to Afghanistan. The reinforcements include combat brigades as well as trainers tasked with expanding and improving Afghan security forces.

The troop increase represents one of the most substantial escalations of the American commitment in Afghanistan since the 2001 invasion that toppled the Taliban regime following the September 11 attacks. Military commanders have long argued that insufficient force levels allowed the insurgency to regroup, particularly in the volatile southern and eastern regions of the country.

A significant portion of the additional forces is aimed at building the capacity of Afghan army and police units — a critical step toward the eventual goal of transferring security responsibilities to Afghan control.

## Tensions Along the Pakistan Border

Gates also addressed the persistent challenges posed by the porous border between Afghanistan and Pakistan, where militants have found sanctuary in the rugged, largely ungoverned tribal areas on the Pakistani side.

The frontier region has long been a source of frustration for American and Afghan officials, who contend that insurgents launch cross-border attacks before retreating to safe havens beyond the reach of coalition forces. The situation has created diplomatic friction, as the United States presses Pakistan to take more aggressive action against militant networks operating within its territory.

Gates recognized the delicate nature of the issue, acknowledging Pakistan's sovereignty concerns while stressing that the safe havens represent a genuine threat to stability on both sides of the border. The interconnected nature of the security challenges has led American officials to increasingly view Afghanistan and Pakistan as a single theater requiring a coordinated regional strategy.

## Looking Ahead

The combination of military reinforcement, potential political reconciliation, and enhanced regional cooperation reflects an evolving understanding of a conflict that has proven far more durable and complex than many anticipated in its early years.

As American forces prepared for the expanded mission, questions remained about how reconciliation might work in practice, whether Pakistan would meaningfully address the border sanctuaries, and how long the additional troops would be required to make a lasting difference.

Gates, who has served under administrations of both parties, has consistently emphasized that there is no purely military solution to the Afghan conflict — a theme that continued to shape his assessment of the road ahead.

---

*This article is a stylistic reconstruction in the format of CNN reporting. For direct quotations and precise figures, readers should consult primary sources and official transcripts.*

# Gates Signals Openness to Afghan Reconciliation as Taliban Sets Preconditions for Talks

**KABUL** — U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates suggested Thursday that political reconciliation with elements of the Taliban could eventually help end the war in Afghanistan, even as a spokesman for the insurgent movement insisted that no negotiations would take place until all foreign troops leave the country.

Speaking to reporters during a visit to Afghanistan, Gates said the United States would support an Afghan-led process to bring willing insurgents back into society, drawing a distinction between hardened ideologues and fighters who might be persuaded to lay down their arms.

"Reconciliation is ultimately going to be part of the solution here," Gates said. "There are undoubtedly people in the Taliban who are fighting for reasons that have nothing to do with ideology — for money, out of intimidation, or because of local grievances. Those are people we believe can be reintegrated."

But Gates cautioned that meaningful talks could only proceed from a position of strength. "Reconciliation on the right terms is something we favor," he said. "But you have to convince the enemy they cannot win before they are willing to seriously talk. That is why the military pressure we are applying now matters so much."

## Taliban Rejects Preconditions

The Taliban, however, offered a starkly different vision of what any political settlement would require. In a statement relayed by telephone, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid dismissed the notion of negotiations while international forces remain on Afghan soil.

"There will be no talks as long as a single foreign soldier remains in our country," Mujahid said. "The occupation must end first. This is not a condition we invented; it is the demand of the Afghan people who are resisting the invaders."

Mujahid rejected the American characterization of insurgents as motivated by money or coercion, framing the fighting as a legitimate struggle. "Our mujahideen are not mercenaries," he said. "They fight for their faith and their homeland. The enemy's talk of reconciliation is propaganda designed to divide us. It will fail."

The spokesman also asserted that the insurgency was growing stronger, contradicting U.S. and NATO claims of battlefield momentum. "Every day our operations expand to new provinces," he said. "The reality on the ground does not match the statements made in Kabul and Washington."

## A War at a Crossroads

The dueling statements underscored the wide gulf between the two sides even as international attention increasingly turns toward how the nearly decade-long conflict might be brought to a close. Western officials have grown more openly supportive of a negotiated outcome, acknowledging that the war is unlikely to be won by military means alone.

Afghan President Hamid Karzai has repeatedly called for reconciliation with insurgents willing to renounce violence, sever ties with al-Qaeda, and accept the Afghan constitution — conditions echoed by U.S. officials.

Gates reiterated those benchmarks on Thursday. "Anyone who wants to be part of Afghanistan's political future has to break with al-Qaeda, put down their weapons, and accept the constitution," he said. "Those are not unreasonable requirements. They are the foundation of any lasting peace."

Analysts remain divided over the prospects for genuine dialogue. Some believe elements of the Taliban's leadership may be quietly probing for a settlement, while others warn that the movement's public demands leave little room for compromise.

Violence has continued unabated across much of southern and eastern Afghanistan, where coalition forces have concentrated operations. Roadside bombs, targeted assassinations, and clashes with insurgents have driven casualties higher, testing public support for the war in Western capitals.

Gates, wrapping up his visit, struck a note of cautious resolve. "No one should expect this to be quick or easy," he said. "But we are making progress, and we intend to see this through in a way that leaves Afghanistan able to secure itself."

For now, the possibility of negotiations appears remote. As Mujahid put it before ending the call: "The path to peace is clear. When the foreigners leave, the fighting will end. Until then, our resistance continues."

---

# Gates Visits Afghanistan, Warns of Tougher Fight Ahead

**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)** -- Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Afghanistan on Thursday to meet with U.S. commanders and troops, cautioning that the escalating fight in the volatile south will likely bring higher American casualties in the months ahead.

The visit comes as thousands of additional U.S. forces flow into the country as part of President Obama's strategy to reverse gains made by a resurgent Taliban, particularly in the southern provinces of Helmand and Kandahar.

"We are entering a very difficult period," Gates told reporters traveling with him. "I think we have to be prepared for the fact that we are going to see higher casualties as we go into these Taliban strongholds. That's just the reality of the fighting that lies ahead."

Gates met with General Stanley McChrystal, the top U.S. and NATO commander in Afghanistan, to discuss the ongoing troop buildup and the broader counterinsurgency strategy. McChrystal has emphasized protecting the Afghan population as central to defeating the insurgency.

## Focus on the South

Much of the increased fighting is concentrated in the south, where U.S. Marines launched a major offensive in Helmand province earlier this summer. The operation, one of the largest since the 2001 invasion, aims to clear Taliban fighters from areas that have been under insurgent influence for years.

The additional forces are part of the roughly 21,000 troops Obama ordered to Afghanistan, bringing the total American presence toward 68,000 by year's end.

Gates acknowledged the challenges of operating in a region where the Taliban maintains deep roots and where progress has been slow.

"The Taliban have had a couple of pretty good years," Gates said. "We have to turn that around, and I think our commanders believe they now have the resources to begin doing that."

## Meeting the Troops

During his visit, Gates planned to meet with service members at several locations to hear directly about conditions on the ground. He praised the resilience of American forces and thanked them for their sacrifices.

The trip also coincides with concerns about mounting violence ahead of Afghanistan's presidential election, with the Taliban vowing to disrupt the vote.

Gates expressed cautious optimism that the new strategy, combined with additional troops and a greater emphasis on training Afghan security forces, would eventually yield results -- though he warned progress would not come quickly or without cost.

"I don't think anyone should expect this to be easy or fast," he said. "But I do believe we now have the right strategy and the right leadership to succeed."

CNN's Pentagon team contributed to this report.
